key_insight: SHROM learns a low-dimensional, invertible latent space for droplet interface shapes by combining shape analysis, neighborhood structure, and an autoencoder so morphology can be represented in a way that is faithful to shape and still reconstructable.
engineering_relevance: This enables more compact surrogate models for fluid-interface dynamics and droplet breakup, supporting faster analysis and interpolation of experimentally observed morphologies without rerunning costly simulations.
method: Represent droplet contours with square-root velocity functions to encode shape.
Build a neighbor graph in shape space and use it as a latent-space regularizer during autoencoder training.
Train an invertible reduced-order model that reconstructs contours while preserving neighborhood structure in latent space.
evidence_signal: The study used 301,539 inkjet droplet contours plus four breakup videos; with the graph regularizer, latent clustering matched the shape-space partition far better (ARI 0.781 ± 0.049 vs 0.063 ± 0.059), while waveform parameters predicted full contours with R² = 0.878 ± 0.026.
watch_item: The method struggles across topology changes, since the regularized latent does not simultaneously represent pre- and post-breakup shapes in one component, and interpolation error is limited by reconstruction accuracy.
paper_title: A shape-similarity latent space for fluid interfaces: invertible reduced-order modelling of droplet morphology
